title: Distributed rate limiter: quotas and fairness
summary: Choose between exact global enforcement and bounded local autonomy.

sections.heading: Define the policy and failure behavior
sections.body: A rate limiter decides whether a unit of work may proceed. The key may be a user, API credential, tenant, endpoint, or a combination. Specify what is counted: requests, bytes, tokens, or weighted cost. Authentication and business authorization remain separate checks. Decide whether a quota is global, per region, or per server, and how much temporary overshoot is acceptable. A limiter protecting an expensive dependency may need conservative failure behavior, while a low-risk public read endpoint may choose availability. There is no universally correct fail-open or fail-closed setting.

sections.heading: Algorithms and a worked token bucket
sections.body: A fixed window is simple but can admit a double burst around a boundary. A sliding log is precise for its window but stores individual events. A token bucket permits bursts while bounding a long-run refill rate. Suppose capacity is 20 tokens and refill is 5 tokens per second. Starting full, 20 unit-cost requests can run immediately. Another request at the same instant is rejected; after 200 milliseconds, one token is available if no other request consumed it. Compute refill from elapsed time, cap at capacity, and subtract cost in one atomic operation. Concurrent read-then-write updates would allow multiple gateways to spend the same tokens.

sections.heading: Central state versus distributed budgets
sections.body: A shared state service can serialize updates for a key and simplify global limits, but adds network latency and becomes a dependency. Partition keys across owners to distribute work, while recognizing that one hot tenant can still overload one key. Regional budgets reduce cross-region coordination: allocate each region part of the total quota and periodically rebalance. The total outstanding allocation must respect the desired bound, including allocations held by failed or disconnected regions. Local fallback buckets provide resilience but can multiply allowed traffic if every gateway independently assumes it owns the full global budget.

sections.heading: Clock, identity, and adversarial inputs
sections.body: Use server-controlled time for refill decisions and avoid trusting client timestamps. Clock differences matter if multiple writers update the same logical bucket, so use a single ownership boundary or an algorithm designed for that environment. Limit the lifetime and cardinality of stored keys; an attacker can otherwise create many unique identities and exhaust memory. IP-based limits can unfairly group users behind shared networks and can be evaded by distributed sources. Layer limits at appropriate scopes rather than treating one key as universal. Rejected requests should include useful retry information without promising a reserved slot in the future.

sections.heading: Lab and operational review
sections.body: Implement a token bucket against a deterministic clock and compare concurrent decisions with a serial reference trace. Test a boundary burst, variable request cost, idle refill, clock anomalies, state-store failure, and a hot key. Calculate worst-case overshoot when five gateways each use a local allowance of ten requests during a shared-store outage. Distinguish that bound from the normal configured quota. Track allowed and denied work, decision latency, per-tenant fairness, and fallback activation. Explain how configuration updates are versioned so a quota change does not leave some gateways applying an obsolete policy indefinitely.

diagram.caption: A gateway selects the quota key and policy, updates bucket state atomically, and returns an admission decision with retry guidance.

questions.q: Why must refill and consumption be atomic?
questions.a: Otherwise concurrent requests can each observe and spend the same available tokens.

questions.q: Does a local limiter enforce a global quota?
questions.a: Only with a budget allocation or coordination scheme; independent full quotas multiply the allowed total.

questions.q: Why can key cardinality become a problem?
questions.a: Every distinct key consumes state, so unbounded client-controlled identities can exhaust the limiter.

lab: Implement a token bucket and calculate the overshoot bound of a five-gateway fallback policy.

title: Enterprise RAG platform: retrieval, access, and evaluation
summary: Design grounded answers over changing private documents with measurable quality.

sections.heading: Begin with a product contract
sections.body: Build an internal question-answering service over documents with changing permissions. The goal is useful answers supported by accessible evidence, not merely fluent text. Specify supported document types, ingestion freshness, tenant isolation, expected latency, and how the system responds when evidence is missing or contradictory. Separate ingestion from serving. A source document has identity, version, access metadata, and deletion status. A chunk inherits that context and includes a stable locator for citations. The model is one component; document quality, retrieval, permissions, and evaluation can dominate whether the system is useful.

sections.heading: Ingestion and retrieval design
sections.body: A connector fetches an authorized source version, extracts text, preserves structure, creates chunks, and writes lexical and vector representations. Record parser and embedding versions so a rebuild can be explained and rolled back. Chunk boundaries should preserve meaning and references instead of blindly cutting every fixed number of characters. At query time, enforce tenant and document access boundaries, retrieve candidates through lexical and semantic paths, rerank when justified, and fit selected evidence into a context budget. A filter applied only after retrieving a few candidates can reduce recall; an access-aware retrieval strategy needs evaluation for both security and quality.

sections.heading: Worked example: an outdated policy
sections.body: A user asks how many days of remote work are permitted. Retrieval finds a current policy allowing two days and an archived policy allowing three. Both documents have similar vocabulary, so similarity alone cannot choose authority. The context builder includes version and effective-date metadata and prefers the current authoritative document under a stated policy. The answer cites the exact supporting passage and can mention that an archived policy differs if useful. If the user loses access before generation, the serving path must not reuse an old unrestricted cached answer. Query, evidence, permission context, and content version all affect cache validity.

sections.heading: Safety, cost, and failure boundaries
sections.body: Retrieved content is untrusted data, including instructions embedded in documents. It must not silently redefine system behavior or grant tool permissions. If the application can take actions, use explicit authorization and bounded tool interfaces outside the language model’s prose. Keep provider credentials on the server and avoid logging sensitive context by default. Apply per-tenant budgets, timeouts, and bounded retries. A fallback to a smaller model may reduce cost but can change answer quality, so evaluate it. A citation that points to a document does not prove the answer is supported; evaluate the relationship between each material claim and its evidence.

sections.heading: Evaluation lab and operations
sections.body: Create a test set covering answerable questions, absent facts, conflicting versions, inaccessible documents, and malicious instructions inside retrieved text. Label relevant evidence separately from expected answer properties. Measure retrieval recall at K, groundedness, usefulness, abstention behavior, permission leakage, latency, and cost per successful task. Compare lexical-only, semantic-only, and hybrid retrieval on the same set. Simulate deletion and permission revocation through the ingestion pipeline and measure propagation. Version prompts, retrieval configuration, indexes, and model choices so regressions can be isolated. Finish by tracing one answer from source version through chunks and retrieval scores to its final citations.

diagram.caption: Authorization constrains retrieval; selected evidence enters a bounded context; generation returns traceable citations or an explicit lack of evidence.

questions.q: Does RAG eliminate hallucinations?
questions.a: No. It supplies evidence, but retrieval errors, misleading context, and unsupported generation still require evaluation and controlled failure behavior.

questions.q: Why include access context in cache design?
questions.a: An answer generated for an authorized user may reveal information to another user or after permissions change.

questions.q: What should be evaluated independently of generation?
questions.a: Whether retrieval finds the right accessible, current evidence for the question.

lab: Create a 20-case evaluation set and compare three retrieval strategies, including inaccessible and contradictory evidence.

title: File sync: manifests, conflicts, and resumable transfer
summary: Separate immutable content from mutable names and version history.

sections.heading: Define the synchronization promise
sections.body: Design personal file storage across a laptop and phone with offline edits, resumable uploads, sharing, and version history. The service should preserve user data when edits conflict, even if it cannot automatically merge every file. Separate file identity from its path: renaming a file should not create unrelated content if stable identity is available. Metadata contains owner, parent directory, name, version, and a manifest of content chunks. Content objects can be immutable and addressed by a strong hash or another stable identifier. The service must still authenticate access; knowing a content identifier is not permission to read it.

sections.heading: Upload and metadata commitment
sections.body: A client detects a local change, computes the new manifest, asks which chunks are missing, and uploads those chunks through resumable operations. After the required content exists, it conditionally commits a new metadata version using the base version it edited. This prevents a partial upload from replacing the visible file with missing bytes. The server records changes in a cursor-based journal so clients can fetch updates incrementally. A client acknowledges a cursor only after it has durably recorded the corresponding local state. Periodic reconciliation handles missed filesystem events and journal retention boundaries.

sections.heading: Worked example: two offline editors
sections.body: Laptop and phone both begin with file version 7. Offline, the laptop changes paragraph one and the phone changes paragraph two. The laptop reconnects and conditionally commits version 8 based on 7. The phone’s commit based on 7 now conflicts. For a plain-text file, a three-way merge may combine changes using version 7 as the base; for a binary file, preserving a conflict copy is often safer. Last-write-wins would be simple but can silently discard one user’s work. The resolution must create a new version and retain enough history to explain what happened.

sections.heading: Deletion, sharing, and garbage collection
sections.body: A deletion needs a tombstone so offline clients learn that the file was removed instead of uploading it again as new. Define how long tombstones and old versions remain available. Garbage collection can remove unreferenced chunks only after considering active versions, pending uploads, retention windows, and shared references. Global deduplication can expose cross-user existence information if the API reveals whether another user owns a chunk, so scope or conceal that behavior carefully. Sharing changes belong to authoritative metadata and must be checked when issuing download access. A cached link needs a stated expiration and revocation contract.

sections.heading: Lab and failure review
sections.body: Build a toy client journal and server version store. Simulate an upload interrupted halfway, a metadata commit retried after a lost response, a rename concurrent with edit, a deleted file on an offline device, and two edits based on the same version. Verify that incomplete chunks never become the visible file. Estimate transfer savings when one chunk changes in a large file, then account for manifest overhead and hash computation. Measure synchronization lag, conflict rate, retries, and orphaned storage. Explain a conservative initial retention policy and how garbage collection proves an object is safe to delete.

diagram.caption: Clients exchange metadata versions, transfer missing immutable chunks, and resolve concurrent file edits explicitly.

questions.q: Why separate content upload from metadata commit?
questions.a: The visible version should change only after all referenced content is available.

questions.q: Why is last-write-wins risky for files?
questions.a: It can silently discard a valid concurrent edit, especially when client clocks differ or edits occurred offline.

questions.q: What does a tombstone solve?
questions.a: It communicates deletion to lagging clients and helps prevent stale copies from reappearing.

lab: Simulate two offline clients editing version 7 and preserve both changes through an explicit conflict policy.

title: Telemetry pipeline: metrics, logs, traces, and overload
summary: Design the monitoring system as a workload with its own failure modes.

sections.heading: Define the questions the system must answer
sections.body: Build a telemetry service that detects customer-impacting failures and supports investigation. Metrics summarize measurements over time; logs record events; traces connect work across service boundaries. They complement each other but have different storage and query patterns. Define acceptable ingestion loss, freshness, retention, and tenant isolation. A useful first requirement is an alert when successful request availability falls below a chosen objective, not a dashboard with every available counter. Telemetry collection must have bounded overhead so an observability outage does not become an application outage.

sections.heading: Collection, buffering, and storage
sections.body: Applications emit bounded records to local or nearby collectors. Collectors batch, compress, attach approved metadata, and forward through a durable buffer when required by the loss budget. Storage paths can differ: a time-series store for aggregate metrics, indexed event storage for logs, and trace-oriented storage for spans. A common correlation identifier links investigations without requiring every log field to become an index. Backpressure policy decides whether to drop, sample, or block under overload. Blocking application requests on a full telemetry queue is usually a deliberate exception, not a harmless default.

sections.heading: Worked cardinality and volume estimate
sections.body: Assume 100 services, each exposing 50 metric names across 20 instances. That gives 100,000 series before other label combinations. Adding a user identifier with one million values can multiply cardinality catastrophically if those combinations are populated. Use bounded labels such as endpoint templates and status classes; keep individual request identifiers in logs or traces when needed. For logs, 10,000 events per second at 500 bytes each produce about 5 MB per second, or 432 GB per day of raw payload. Compression, replication, indexes, and retention change physical storage, so state those multipliers separately rather than hiding them.

sections.heading: Sampling, alerts, and failures
sections.body: Head sampling decides early which traces to retain and can cheaply bound volume, but it may miss rare failures. Tail sampling uses completed-trace information to keep interesting cases, at the cost of buffering, coordination, and waiting. Neither should quietly bias a metric used as an exact denominator. Alert on symptoms with actionable ownership and include enough context for investigation. A traffic drop to zero can mean no users or broken collection, so monitor the telemetry pipeline itself and distinguish missing data from successful requests. Keep a minimal independent health signal for major pipeline failures.

sections.heading: Lab and operational review
sections.body: Design one availability alert and one latency alert with explicit windows and missing-data behavior. Generate a traffic trace with a short spike, sustained failure, and collector outage; show which conditions page an operator. Calculate storage for seven days of logs under a stated compression and replication assumption. Add one unbounded label and explain how you detect and contain the resulting series growth. Measure ingestion lag, rejected records, buffer age, query latency, and alert delay. Finish with a runbook that connects a customer symptom to metrics, a trace, and relevant logs without exposing unnecessary sensitive payloads.

diagram.caption: Collectors batch and bound telemetry; storage serves investigations and alerting without making application health depend on telemetry health.

questions.q: Why can metric labels be more dangerous than metric names?
questions.a: Each populated combination creates another series; an unbounded label can multiply state and indexing cost.

questions.q: Does absence of errors prove health?
questions.a: No. Traffic or telemetry collection may be missing, so missing data needs explicit interpretation.

questions.q: Why separate telemetry buffering from application success?
questions.a: A monitoring outage should not automatically block the application’s primary work; any stronger delivery guarantee needs an explicit tradeoff.

lab: Design a bounded telemetry pipeline and evaluate an alert against spikes, sustained failure, and missing data.
